newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Asia chip shares unaffected by book-to-bill rise.
newsitem.headline: Asia chip shares unaffected by book-to-bill rise.

text.p: A rise in the semiconductor industry's key indicator -- the U.S. book-to-bill ratio -- prompted scant reaction in Asian stock markets, but drew a welcome response from industry analysts.
The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said on Tuesday that the book-to-bill ratio rose to 0.99 in September -- a new year high, from a revised 0.93 in August.
The ratio means manufacturers received US$99 in new orders last month for every US$100 in shipments.
"The figure is almost in line with what was estimated and that shows that the semiconductor business is in a recovery trend," said Hiroyuki Iba, a Nikko Research Centre analyst.
Industry analysts expected the ratio to inch closer to the breakeven level with most estimates averaging around 0.95.
Worldwide, the ratio rose to 0.97 in August, from 0.95 in July. Global figures include Asia, Europe, North America and Japan.
Recent improvements in the index have prompted a rally in semiconductor stocks in the region, where many economies rely on these exports for growth.
But these centres -- such as Tokyo and Taipei -- were focused on other factors on Wednesday, limiting the response in the market.

South Korea, where semiconductors account for almost 20 percent of exports, was an exception in early trading. Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics rode on the book-to-bill ratio rise in early trade.
In Singapore, analysts said a strong U.S. semiconductor industry bodes well for the island state's industry, but that any revival is not likely until the first quarter of 1997.

"I think the real rally in the electronics sector will come towards the first quarter of 1997. Then demand will be driven by new technology, new markets and new distribution channels," said Winston Lim, electronics analyst at DBS Securities.
"By the time the new orders get translated into increased output here, it will be six months...sometime in the first quarter of next year," said Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at JM Sassoon.
But some analysts linked the book-to-bill ratio increase to seasonal factors which would be difficult to maintain.

"It's not that impressive because it's a temporary demand for PCs ahead of the Christmas season," said analyst Park Ki-pyong of Hanyang Securities. "The ratio rose due to a reduction in supply, not from a rise in demand."

The book-to-bill ratio, a leading indicator of future demand tallied by the SIA trade group, has been improving recently, reflecting an increase in orders by personal computer makers and more stable prices for memory chips.

Prices of dynamic random access memory chips, or DRAMs, had plummeted during the year to a fraction of what they were in January. But since mid-September, memory prices have risen 30 to 50 percent from their lows.
